texts.facts: 1. By way of present appeal, the appellant/respondent no.1 has assailed the Judgment of Ld. Trial Court dated 27.04.2015 in complaint case filed u/s 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act). Sh. Dal Chand @ Hemant vs Smt. Madhu Rani on 17 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44019045/ 1 The appellant was also restrained from committing any further act of domestic violence and also restrained from causing harassment and cruelty to the respondent no. 1. 2. The facts of the case giving rise to the filing of appeal are that the marriage of appellant and complainant was solemnized on 8.12.2008 according to Hindu rites and customs and one child was born out of the wedlock namely Master Davesh / respondent no. 2. It is also alleged that since the day of marriage, the behaviour of appellant and his family members was not good towards respondent no. 1 as they were not happy with the dowry articles given by the parents of respondent no. 1 and they taunted respondent no. 1 and pressurized her to bring more dowry. It is further stated that parents of CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 2 respondent no. 1 spent Rs.7 lakhs in the marriage. It is also stated that parents, brothers and sisters of the appellant instigated the appellant to beat the respondent no. 1 and pressurize her to bring more dowry. It is further stated that respondent no. 1 was treated with cruelty and also beaten for not fulfilling the dowry demands. It is also stated that appellant used to give beating to respondent no. 1 during her pregnancy. It is also averred that appellant and his family had thrown out respondent no. 1 of the matrimonial home. It is further averred that aggrieved by the behaviour of the appellant and his family members, respondent no. 1 lodged a complaint in Crime Against Women Cell against the appellant and his family members where the matter was compromised and respondent no. 1 returned to the matrimonial home and started residing in a rented accommodation with appellant. However, the appellant even thereafter continued to treat the respondent no. 1 with cruelty. It is also stated that on an objection raised by respondent no. 1 regarding his illicit relations, appellant poured kerosene oil on himself and called the police and threatened to falsely implicate the respondent no.1. It is further alleged that after the said incident, the parents of respondent no. 1 brought her back to her parental home. 3. It is further stated that appellant has not made any provision CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 3 for the livelihood of the respondents and respondent no. 1 is totally dependent on her parents. It is also stated that appellant has neglected and refused to maintain the respondent, though he was a man of means and earning Rs.50,000/ per month from his computer business. It is prayed that protection order and residence order be passed and respondents be granted monetary relief as well as compensation/damages. 4. Appellant/respondent filed written statement opposing the complainant taking preliminary objections that the petition was an abuse of the process of law as respondent/complainant no.1 had impleaded three women namely respondent no. 3, 5 and 6 even though the Act provides that no woman can be made a party. It was further stated that respondent no. 1 had concealed true facts from the court and had made allegations which were contradictory to the allegations made in the petition u/s 125 Cr.P.C. It was further stated that the marriage of of appellant and respondent no. 1 was a simple one without exchange of any dowry / gift or cash. 5. It was also stated that since the date of marriage, the behaviour of respondent no. 1 was very cruel towards the appellant and his family members. It was also stated that respondent no. 1 filed CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 4 a false complaint against the appellant and his family members in the Crime against Women Cell and before the Women Commission, Delhi. Sh. Dal Chand @ Hemant vs Smt. Madhu Rani on 17 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44019045/ 2 6. It was further stated that respondent no. 1 had threatened to make the life of appellant and his family members hell in case the first floor of the property / dwelling house of appellant and his family member was not transferred in her name. It was also alleged that respondent no. 1 did not allow the child to meet the grand parents. It was further averred that seeing the conduct of respondent no. 1, the father of appellant disowned and disinherited him (appellant). It was further stated that respondent no. 1 extended threats to kill the family members of appellant. 7. On merits, it was admitted that marriage of the parties was solemnized according to the Hindu rites and customs. It was denied that Rs.7 lakhs were spent in the marriage by the parents of respondent no. 1. It was reiterated that marriage was a simple one. It was denied that appellant and his family treated the respondent no. 1 with cruelty for dowry demands and pressurized her to bring more dowry. It was also denied that the appellant or his family members gave beatings to respondent during her pregnancy. It was stated that pursuant to CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 5 compromise arrived at in the CAW cell, the appellant had taken a rented accommodation and respondent no. 1 shifted therein with all her dowry, istridhan and jewellery. It was also denied that appellant had illicit relations or that on an objection of respondent no. 1 to his illicit relations, he (appellant) poured kerosene oil on himself and called the police and threatened to falsely implicate the respondent no. 1. It was stated that in fact respondent no. 1 had intoxicated the appellant and poured kerosene oil on him and tried to set him on fire. It was denied that respondent no.1 was forced to leave the matrimonial home due to cruelty of the appellant and his family members. It was stated that respondent no. 1 left matrimonial home on her own. 8. The impugned order has been challenged on the ground that respondent no. 1 is neither a man of means nor is he running business of computer hardware and earning Rs. 50,000/ per month as alleged. It was contended that appellant was an employee in M/s R.K. Computers and Mobiles but had left the job as the said firm shifted to Gurgaon. It was further stated that appellant was unemployed and had no source of income. It was also contended that respondent no. 1 is not dependent on her parents but is qualified and giving tuition and earning Rs.5000/ per month. 12. It was further stated that the impugned order had been passed after appreciating facts, documents and evidence. The respondent no.1 had filed details of business of appellant i.e., the visiting card, details of business of appellant on website of Google and Just Dial. The respondents being aggrieved by the cruelty of appellant and his family members and as the appellant failed to make any provision for their livelihood filed a complaint u/s 12, 18, 19, 20 & 22 of the Act. However, Ld. Trial Court declined the prayer for declaring family of appellant as a shared household. 21. The respondent examined herself as CW1 and file her evidence by affidavit stating stated that she had no source of income. She also stated that she was forced to leave the matrimonial home on account of cruelty of appellant and his family members. She further stated that the appellant had not made any provision for the maintenance of the CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 17 respondents. She also stated that appellant was a man of means as he was running business of computer service centre and he had no other liability or responsibility. The complainant Sh. Dal Chand @ Hemant vs Smt. Madhu Rani on 17 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44019045/ 8 had proved the visiting card of appellant Ex.PW1/16. The complainant also filed the details of business of appellant available on the website of Google and Just Dial as Ex.PW1/17 and Ex.PW1/18. In her crossexamination, she had stated that she was educated up to 11th standard and was unemployed whereas her husband was earning Rs. 50,000/ from the business of selling hardware products. She denied that Ex. PW1/16, Ex. PW1/A and Ex. PW18 were false and fabricated.

Madhu Rani & Ors. 7 earning about Rs.8000/ per month by doing casual jobs out of which he had to pay Rs.2500/ for the rented accommodation. It was also stated that appellant could not produce the rent receipt or any rent agreement as the landlord did not issue a rent receipt nor had executed a rent agreement. It was further stated that appellant could not furnish the name of his employer as he was a daily wager. It was also stated that appellant was educated up to 9th standard and respondent no. 1 had admitted that appellant did not have any engineering degree or diploma. Thus, the appellant was an unskilled worker and as per the minimum wages Act, the income of unskilled worker could not be more than Rs.7000 to Rs.8000/. It was further stated that Ld. Trial Court grossly erred in awarding maintenance of Rs.10000/ per month to the respondents which includes the rent for suitable accommodation whereas in fact, respondent no. 1 was residing with her parents. 11. Respondents filed reply to the petition stating that appeal was not maintainable as it was filed beyond the period of limitation. It was also stated that appellant had suppressed material facts from court. It was also stated that parents of appellant had spent Rs.7 lakhs in her marriage. It CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 8 was also alleged that appellant failed to prove that the respondent no. 1 had capacity to earn livelihood for herself and her child. It was also stated that appellant had failed to prove that he was employed with M/s R.K. Computers and Mobiles on a monthly salary of Rs.4,500/ per month and he lost the job. It was also alleged that appellant had also not filed any documentary proof of the rent being paid by him. It was denied that respondents levelled false allegations of cruelty meted out to her against appellant and his family members. The averments made in the complaint were reiterated in the reply. Section 29 of the Act provides that an appeal has to be filed within 30 days of the order. CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 9 15. Now coming to the merits of the case, Section 12 of Act provides that an aggrieved person or any person on behalf of aggrieved person or a Protection Officer on behalf of aggrieved person may present an application to the Magistrate seeking one or more reliefs as provided thereunder, is as follows: Sh. Dal Chand @ Hemant vs Smt. Madhu Rani on 17 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44019045/ 4 "12. Application to Magistrate. (1) An aggrieved person or a Protection Officer or any other person on behalf of the aggrieved person may present an application to the Magistrate seeking one or more reliefs under this Act: Provided that before passing any order on such application, the Magistrate shall take into consideration any domestic incident report received by him from the Protection Officer or the service provider. (2) The relief sought for under subsection (1) may include a relief for issuance of an order for payment of compensation or damages without prejudice to the right of such person to institute a suit for compensation or damages for the injuries caused by the acts of domestic violence committed by the respondent: Provided that where a decree for any amount as compensation or damages has been passed by any Court in favour of the aggrieved person, the amount, if any, paid or payable in pursuance of the order made by the Magistrate CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 10 under this Act shall be set off against the amount payable under such decree and the decree shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), or any other law for the time being in force, be executable for the balance amount, if any, left after such set off. (3) Every application under subsection (1) shall be in such form and contain such particulars as may be prescribed or as nearly as possible thereto. (4) The Magistrate shall fix the first date of hearing, which shall not ordinarily be beyond three days from the date of receipt of the application by the Court. (5) The Magistrate shall endeavour to dispose of every application made under sub section (1) within a period of sixty days from the date of its first hearing." 16. Section 18 of the Act relates to protection order and is as follows: "Protection Orders. The Magistrate may, after giving the aggrieved person and the respondent an opportunity of being heard and on being prima facie satisfied that domestic violence has taken place or is likely to take place, pass a protection order in favour of the aggrieved person and prohibit the respondent from CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 11 (a) committing any act of domestic violence; (b) aiding or abetting in the commission of acts of domestic violence; (c) entering the place of employment of the aggrieved person or, if the person aggrieved is a child, its school or any other place frequented by the aggrieved person; Sh. Dal Chand @ Hemant vs Smt. Madhu Rani on 17 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44019045/ 5 ( d) attempting to communicate in any form, whatsoever, with the aggrieved person, including personal, oral or written or electronic or telephonic contact; (e) alienating any assets, operating bank lockers or bank accounts used or held or enjoyed by both the parties, jointly by the aggrieved person and the respondent or singly by the respondent, including her stridhan or any other property held either jointly by the parties or separately by them without the leave of the Magistrate; (f) causing violence to the dependants, other relatives or any person who give the aggrieved person assistance from domestic violence; (g) committing any other act as specified in the protection order. 17. Section 19 of the Act relates to Residence Orders and provides as under: (1) While disposing of an application under subsection (1) of section 12, the Magistrate may, on being satisfied that domestic violence CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 12 has taken place, pass a residence order (a) restraining the respondent from dispossessing or in any other manner disturbing the possession of the aggrieved person from the shared household, whether or not the respondent has a legal or equitable interest in the shared household; (b) directing the respondent to remove himself from the shared household, whether or not the respondent has a legal or equitable interest in the shared household; (c) restraining the respondent or any of his relatives from entering any portion of the shared household in which the aggrieved person resides; (d) restraining the respondent from alienating or disposing off the shared household or encumbering the same; (e) restraining the respondent from renouncing his rights in the shared household except with the leave of the Magistrate; or (f) directing the respondent to secure same level of alternate accommodation for the aggrieved person as enjoyed by her in the shared household o th pay rent for the same, f the circumstances so require: Provided that no order under clause (b) shall be passed against any person who is a woman. (2) The Magistrate may impose any additional conditions or pass any other direction which he may deem reasonably necessary to protect or to CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Sh. Dal Chand @ Hemant vs Smt. Madhu Rani on 17 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44019045/ 6 Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 13 provide for the safety of the aggrieved person or any child of such aggrieved person. (3) The Magistrate may require from the respondent to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for preventing the commission of domestic violence. (4) An order under subsection (3) shall be deemed to be an order under Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) and shall be dealt with accordingly. (5) While passing an order under subsection (1), subsection (2) or subsection (3), the Court may also pass an order directing the officer in charge of the nearest police station to give protection to the aggrieved person or to assist her or the person making an application on her behalf in the implementation of the order. (6) While making an order under subsection (1), the Magistrate may impose on the respondent obligations relating to the discharge of rent and other payments, having regard to the financial needs and resources of the parties. (7) The Magistrate may direct the officer in charge of the police station in whose jurisdiction the Magistrate has been approached to assist in the implementation of the protection order. (8) The Magistrate may direct the respondent to return to the possession of the aggrieved person her stridhan or any other property or valuable security to which she is entitled to . CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 14 18. Section 20 of the Act relates to Monetary Reliefs, the same is as under: (1) While disposing of an application under subsection (1) of section 12, the Magistrate may direct the respondent to pay monetary relief to meet the expenses incurred and losses suffered by the aggrieved person and any child of the aggrieved person as a result of the domestic violence and such relief may include, but not limited to, (a) the loss of earnings; (b) the medical expenses; (c) The loss caused due to the destruction, damage or removal of any property from the control of the aggrieved person; and (d) the maintenance for the aggrieved person as well as her children, if any, including an order under or in addition to an order of maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) or any other law for the time being in force. (3) The Magistrate shall have the power to order an appropriate lump sum payment or monthly payments of maintenance, as the nature and circumstances of the case may require. (4) The Magistrate shall send a copy of the CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 15 order for monetary relief made under sub section (1) to the parties to the application and to the in charge of the police station within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the respondent resides. (5) The respondent shall pay the monetary relief granted to the aggrieved person within the period specified in the order under sub section (1). (6) Upon the failure on the part of the respondent to make payment in terms of the order under subsection (1), the Magistrate may direct the employer or a debtor of the respondent, to directly pay to the aggrieved person or to deposit with the court a portion of the wages or salaries or debt due to or accrued to the credit of the respondent, which amount may be adjusted towards the monetary relief payable by the respondent." 19. Madhu Rani & Ors. 15 order for monetary relief made under sub section (1) to the parties to the application and to the in charge of the police station within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the respondent resides. (5) The respondent shall pay the monetary relief granted to the aggrieved person within the period specified in the order under sub section (1). (6) Upon the failure on the part of the respondent to make payment in terms of the order under subsection (1), the Magistrate may direct the employer or a debtor of the respondent, to directly pay to the aggrieved person or to deposit with the court a portion of the wages or salaries or debt due to or accrued to the credit of the respondent, which amount may be adjusted towards the monetary relief payable by the respondent." 19. Section 22 of the Act relates to Compensation Orders and provides as under: "In addition to other reliefs as may be granted under this Act, the Magistrate may on an application being made by the aggrieved person, pass an order directing the respondent to pay compensation and damages for the injuries, including mental torture and emotional distress, caused by the facts of CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 16 domestic violence committed by that respondent." 20. CA No. 05/15 Dal Chand @ Hemant Vs. Madhu Rani & Ors. 20 25.
